title: unsafe & Pointer Arithmetic
summary: The `unsafe` package is Go's escape hatch from the type system. `unsafe.Pointer` can convert between unrelated pointer types, and combined with `uintptr` it enables raw pointer arithmetic. It unlocks zero-copy conversions and tight struct layout — but it bypasses every safety guarantee, so a single mistake means memory corruption.

subtopics.title: unsafe.Pointer as a universal pointer
subtopics.explanation: An unsafe.Pointer can hold a pointer of any type and be converted to a pointer of any other type. It's the only legal bridge between, say, *int and *float64. The conversions are checked by no one — correctness is entirely your responsibility.

subtopics.title: uintptr and pointer arithmetic
subtopics.explanation: uintptr is an integer big enough to hold a pointer's bits. Converting unsafe.Pointer to uintptr lets you do arithmetic (add an offset), then convert back. Crucially, a uintptr is NOT a pointer — the garbage collector ignores it, so it must never be stored across a statement boundary.

subtopics.title: Sizeof, Alignof, Offsetof
subtopics.explanation: unsafe.Sizeof gives a type's size in bytes, Alignof its required alignment, and Offsetof the byte offset of a struct field. These are compile-time constants used to compute layouts and field addresses precisely.
subtopics.example: unsafe.Offsetof(s.B) // bytes from start of s to B

subtopics.title: Struct padding & alignment
subtopics.explanation: The compiler inserts padding so each field meets its alignment requirement. Reordering fields large-to-small can shrink a struct. unsafe.Sizeof/Offsetof let you measure and exploit this layout exactly.
subtopics.example: struct{a bool; _ [7]byte; b int64} // explicit padding

subtopics.title: The GC rule: don't stash a uintptr
subtopics.explanation: Go's garbage collector can move objects and only tracks real pointers. A uintptr holding an address is invisible to it: if the object moves or is freed, your uintptr dangles. Pointer arithmetic must be done in a single expression, converting back to unsafe.Pointer immediately.
subtopics.example: unsafe.Pointer(uintptr(p) + off) // all in one expression

subtopics.title: unsafe.Slice & unsafe.String
subtopics.explanation: Go 1.17+ added unsafe.Add and Go 1.20 added unsafe.Slice and unsafe.String, giving safer, clearer ways to build a slice/string from a base pointer and length than hand-rolling header structs — still unsafe, but less error-prone.

foundations.overview: Go is a memory-safe language: the type system and garbage collector conspire to make dangling pointers and type confusion impossible. The unsafe package deliberately removes those guardrails. With unsafe.Pointer you can reinterpret one type's bytes as another; with uintptr you can do raw address arithmetic. This is exactly what low-level libraries, zero-copy conversions, and cgo need — and exactly what will silently corrupt memory if you get the rules wrong.
foundations.formalDefinition: unsafe is a compiler-recognized package providing unsafe.Pointer (a pointer type convertible to/from any pointer type and uintptr) plus the compile-time functions Sizeof, Alignof, Offsetof, and (in modern Go) Add, Slice, and String. It permits operations the type system otherwise forbids, with no runtime checks.
foundations.whyItMatters: unsafe powers high-performance, low-level Go: zero-copy []byte to string conversions, struct field access in serialization, interop with C via cgo, and memory-mapped layouts. Knowing its strict rules — especially the uintptr/GC rule — is what separates a working optimization from an intermittent crash.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of Go's type system as a sealed nuclear reactor with safety interlocks. unsafe is the override key that disables the interlocks: useful for the rare maintenance task, catastrophic if you forget to turn them back on. uintptr is a photograph of a pipe's location — useful for a split second, but if the reactor is rearranged (GC moves objects), the photo points at the wrong place.
foundations.runtimePerspective: The compiler treats unsafe.Pointer specially: it remains a real pointer that the garbage collector tracks and updates if the object moves. uintptr does NOT — it's a plain integer the GC ignores. So if you convert a pointer to uintptr, do arithmetic, and the GC runs in between, the object may have moved (or been collected) and your integer is now garbage. The rule is to convert pointer to uintptr, add, and convert back to unsafe.Pointer all within one expression.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Zero-copy string([]byte) conversions in hot paths, reading fields from packed binary structs, atomic operations on arbitrary types, cgo data exchange, and tightly packing structs by understanding alignment.
foundations.businessImpact: A correctly applied zero-copy conversion can remove a major allocation/copy in a hot path, cutting CPU and GC pressure and thus machine count — but a single unsafe bug can cause hard-to-reproduce crashes that cost far more to debug.
foundations.engineeringImpact: unsafe code can't be checked by the compiler or, fully, the race detector; it demands isolation, heavy commenting, and tests, and it ties you to Go's (intentionally minimal) compatibility promise for the package.
foundations.performanceImpact: It can eliminate copies and allocations entirely (e.g. []byte<->string without copying), but the savings only matter on genuine hot paths; elsewhere the risk outweighs the gain.
commonUseCases: Reading fields from packed binary/wire formats

commonMisconceptions.myth: uintptr is just another pointer type, so I can store it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: uintptr is an integer the GC ignores. Stored across statements, it can dangle if the object moves or is freed. Do arithmetic in a single expression.

commonMisconceptions.myth: unsafe conversions are free and always safe if they compile.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The compiler does not validate that the bytes are a valid value of the target type or that lifetimes line up; misuse corrupts memory silently.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Struct field order doesn't affect size.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Alignment padding means reordering fields large-to-small can shrink a struct measurably — visible via unsafe.Sizeof.

visualExplorer.title: Safe pointer arithmetic to a struct field
visualExplorer.caption: The single-expression rule that keeps the GC from invalidating your pointer.

config.intro: Reading a field via unsafe, done correctly:

steps.name: Take a real pointer
steps.detail: p := unsafe.Pointer(&s) — a tracked pointer to the struct; the GC will update it if s moves.

steps.name: Get the offset
steps.detail: off := unsafe.Offsetof(s.Field) — a compile-time constant number of bytes from the struct's start.

steps.name: Arithmetic in ONE expression
steps.detail: fp := unsafe.Pointer(uintptr(p) + off) — convert to uintptr, add, convert back, all without a statement boundary.

steps.name: Reinterpret
steps.detail: v := (*T)(fp) — treat that address as a *T to read/write the field.

steps.name: Never stash the uintptr
steps.detail: If you saved uintptr(p) in a variable and the GC moved s, that integer would now point at freed/moved memory.

visualExplorer.title: Why []byte and string share a layout
visualExplorer.caption: A string header is {ptr, len} and a slice header is {ptr, len, cap}. Because the first two words line up, unsafe lets you reinterpret a []byte as a string (and vice versa) without copying the bytes — the basis of zero-copy conversion.

interactiveExamples.title: Measure struct layout with Sizeof and Offsetof
interactiveExamples.explanation: Alignment padding makes field order matter. Sizeof reports total size; Offsetof reports each field's byte offset. Notice the padding inserted to align the int64.

code.expectedOutput:
size: 24
off A: 0
off B: 8

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: zero-copy []byte to string
interactiveExamples.explanation: Converting []byte to string normally copies. Using unsafe (Go 1.20 unsafe.String) you can share the backing array. The starter still copies — replace it with the zero-copy form. (Caution: the resulting string must not be used after the slice is mutated/freed.)

interactiveExamples.title: Read a struct field via pointer arithmetic (the right way)
interactiveExamples.explanation: We compute the field's address with the single-expression rule: pointer -> uintptr -> add offset -> back to unsafe.Pointer, never stashing the uintptr. Then reinterpret as *int64.

checkpoints.prompt: This computes a field address but can crash intermittently. What's the rule it violates?
checkpoints.code:
base := uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&s)) // stored as uintptr
runSomethingThatMayGC()
fp := unsafe.Pointer(base + unsafe.Offsetof(s.B))
options: It stores an address as uintptr across statements; if the GC moves s, base is stale
checkpoints.explanation: A uintptr is an integer the GC ignores. Storing the address in `base` and using it after a GC may run means s could have moved, leaving base pointing at the wrong (or freed) memory. The arithmetic must happen in a single expression: unsafe.Pointer(uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&s)) + off).

checkpoints.prompt: Given the struct below, what does unsafe.Sizeof print on a 64-bit machine?
checkpoints.explanation: b needs 8-byte alignment, so 7 bytes of padding follow a (offset 8). After c at offset 16, the struct is padded to a multiple of its 8-byte alignment, giving 24. Reordering to b, a, c would shrink it to 16.

checkpoints.prompt: Which conversions does Go guarantee are valid with unsafe.Pointer?
options: Any *T1 to any *T2 with no caveats
unsafe.Pointer <-> any pointer type, and unsafe.Pointer <-> uintptr, following the documented patterns
checkpoints.explanation: unsafe.Pointer is the legal bridge to/from any pointer type and to/from uintptr. But the conversions are only *correct* if you follow the documented patterns (e.g. single-expression arithmetic, compatible layouts); the compiler won't stop an incorrect one.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the single-expression pointer arithmetic to reach field B safely.
checkpoints.explanation: You must convert to uintptr, add the offset, and convert back to unsafe.Pointer in one expression. unsafe.Pointer can't be added directly, and leaving the result as a uintptr would violate the GC rule.

codeLab.title: Zero-copy string<->[]byte (correctly)
codeLab.instructions: Implement `StringToBytes(s string) []byte` and `BytesToString(b []byte) string` that share the backing memory without copying, using the Go 1.20 helpers unsafe.String/unsafe.Slice. Handle the empty case. The reflect-based harness verifies the contents match AND that the byte slice shares the string's backing pointer (no copy).
hints: Use unsafe.StringData(s) to get the *byte at the start of a string (Go 1.20+).
unsafe.Slice(ptr, n) builds a []byte header over n bytes starting at ptr — no copy.
unsafe.String(&b[0], n) builds a string header over b's bytes — no copy.
Guard the empty case: &b[0] would panic on a length-0 slice.

debuggingLab.title: Pointer arithmetic that corrupts under GC pressure
debuggingLab.symptom: A function reading struct fields via unsafe usually works but occasionally returns garbage or crashes under load.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The address is stored in a uintptr (a plain integer) across statement boundaries. The garbage collector can move the object that s points to between (1) and (2); it updates real pointers but not integers, so `addr` becomes stale and the later dereference reads moved or freed memory. The bug is timing-dependent, hence intermittent.
commonMistakes: Saving uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(x)) in a variable and reusing it later.
Performing pointer arithmetic across multiple statements.
Assuming the GC never moves objects.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Do the conversion and arithmetic in a single expression so no uintptr survives a statement boundary.

theory.question: What is the difference between unsafe.Pointer and uintptr, and why does it matter for the garbage collector?
theory.directAnswer: unsafe.Pointer is a real pointer that the garbage collector tracks and updates if the object moves; it's the legal bridge between pointer types. uintptr is just an integer holding an address — the GC ignores it. So if you convert a pointer to uintptr, the GC can move or free the object and your integer becomes a stale address. The rule is to do any pointer arithmetic in a single expression: convert pointer→uintptr, add the offset, convert back to unsafe.Pointer, with no statement boundary in between.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways to hold an address — one GC-aware (unsafe.Pointer), one not (uintptr).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: unsafe.Pointer enables type punning safely w.r.t. GC; uintptr enables arithmetic, which pointers can't do directly.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The GC scans stacks/heaps for real pointers and rewrites them on a move; it can't know an integer is secretly an address.

theory.whyImportant: Misusing uintptr is the canonical unsafe bug — intermittent and brutal to debug.
theory.realWorldExample: Computing a struct field's address: must be one expression, never a stored uintptr.

followUps.question: Does Go's GC actually move objects?
followUps.answer: Stacks can move (growable goroutine stacks), so stack-allocated objects relocate; the contiguous heap doesn't compact today, but the rules are written so code stays correct if it ever does.

followUps.question: What's unsafe.Add for?
followUps.answer: Go 1.17+ unsafe.Add(ptr, len) does the offset arithmetic for you on an unsafe.Pointer, clearer and safer than manual uintptr math.

theory.question: How does struct alignment and padding affect memory layout, and how would you measure and optimize it?
theory.directAnswer: Each field must sit at an offset that's a multiple of its alignment (e.g. int64 needs 8-byte alignment), so the compiler inserts padding between fields and at the end. This can make a struct much larger than the sum of its fields. Measure with unsafe.Sizeof, unsafe.Alignof, and unsafe.Offsetof; optimize by ordering fields from largest to smallest alignment, which minimizes padding. Tools like fieldalignment automate the check.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The rules governing where fields land in memory and how big a struct is.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Hardware accesses aligned data faster (or requires alignment); the compiler honors that with padding.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Sizeof/Alignof/Offsetof are compile-time constants exposing the layout the compiler chose.

theory.whyImportant: Layout matters for memory footprint at scale and for matching C/wire formats.
theory.realWorldExample: Reordering a hot struct from {bool,int64,bool} to {int64,bool,bool} shrinks it from 24 to 16 bytes.

followUps.question: How do you find badly-aligned structs automatically?
followUps.answer: Run `go vet -vettool=$(which fieldalignment)` or the fieldalignment analyzer, which flags structs that could be smaller.

followUps.question: Why might you NOT reorder for size?
followUps.answer: Readability or a required layout (e.g. matching a C struct or wire protocol) can outweigh the savings.

scenario.question: A teammate added an unsafe []byte-to-string conversion to remove an allocation in a hot path, and now you get rare, baffling corruption far from that code. What's the likely cause and how do you make it safe?
scenario.directAnswer: The zero-copy conversion makes the string share the slice's backing array. If anything mutates or reuses that []byte (e.g. a pooled buffer) while the string is still referenced, the string's bytes change underneath it — corruption that surfaces elsewhere. Make it safe by guaranteeing the byte slice is immutable for the string's entire lifetime (never write to it, never return it to a pool), document the invariant loudly, or simply copy on the rare boundary where lifetimes can't be guaranteed.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A lifetime/aliasing hazard from sharing a mutable backing array as an immutable string.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Strings are assumed immutable; the zero-copy trick breaks that assumption if the slice changes.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Both views point at the same bytes; mutating one silently mutates the other.

scenario.whyImportant: Zero-copy unsafe conversions are a classic source of action-at-a-distance bugs.
scenario.realWorldExample: A sync.Pool buffer reused for the next request mutated bytes still referenced by a cached string from the previous request.

followUps.question: Where is the zero-copy trick actually safe?
followUps.answer: When the bytes are provably immutable for the string's lifetime — e.g. read-only request data that's never written or pooled.

followUps.question: How would you catch this in testing?
followUps.answer: Stress with the -race detector and randomized buffer reuse; mutate buffers aggressively in tests to surface aliasing.

coding.question: Implement `func ReadUint32LE(b []byte) uint32` that interprets the first 4 bytes as a little-endian uint32 with zero copies, using unsafe — and explain why encoding/binary is usually the better choice.
coding.thoughtProcess: On a little-endian machine, the four bytes already lay out as a uint32, so we can reinterpret &b[0] as a *uint32 and dereference. We must bounds-check first (len >= 4) since unsafe skips that. Crucially this only works on little-endian hardware — which is why encoding/binary.LittleEndian.Uint32 (which assembles bytes explicitly) is portable and the idiomatic choice.
coding.lineByLine: We bounds-check manually because unsafe performs no checks — reading past the slice would corrupt memory. &b[0] is the address of the first byte; casting it to *uint32 and dereferencing reads four bytes as a native-endian integer. On little-endian CPUs that equals the little-endian value. The comment flags the portability trap: on a big-endian machine this returns the byte-swapped result, so encoding/binary, which composes the value byte by byte, is the safe, portable answer.

followUps.question: Why is encoding/binary preferred despite being 'slower'?
followUps.answer: It's portable across endianness and bounds-safe, and the compiler often optimizes it well; correctness beats a tiny, fragile unsafe win.

followUps.question: How could the unsafe version still go wrong on little-endian?
followUps.answer: If &b[0] isn't 4-byte aligned on a platform that requires alignment, the load can fault; slices from byte streams aren't guaranteed aligned.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Quarantine unsafe behind a tiny, well-tested package with a safe typed API; the rest of the codebase never imports unsafe directly. Document every invariant (lifetimes, alignment, endianness) at the call site.
productionDeepDive.performance: unsafe pays off only on real hot paths — zero-copy conversions and packed layouts that profiling shows matter. Elsewhere the maintenance and crash risk dwarfs the nanoseconds saved.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: The race detector can't fully see through unsafe pointer punning, and zero-copy aliasing creates shared mutable state. Treat unsafe-shared memory as you would any shared state: synchronize or keep it provably immutable.
productionDeepDive.reliability: unsafe bugs are intermittent (GC timing) and corrupt memory far from their cause. Follow the documented unsafe.Pointer patterns exactly, keep arithmetic in single expressions, and add stress tests with -race.
productionDeepDive.observability: There's no runtime safety net, so invest in tests and static analysis: `go vet`, the fieldalignment analyzer, and fuzzing of any byte-reinterpretation code.
productionDeepDive.security: Reinterpreting attacker-controlled bytes as typed structures can read out of bounds or violate invariants; always bounds-check and validate before any unsafe reinterpretation of untrusted input.

caseStudies.solution: Carefully reviewed unsafe.String/Slice usage gated behind safe APIs.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Maximum speed vs. extreme care and minimal compatibility guarantees for unsafe.
caseStudies.lessons: Confine unsafe to tiny, audited helpers with documented invariants.

caseStudies.problem: Allocation and copy overhead dominated decode hot paths.
caseStudies.solution: Zero-copy []byte<->string and direct field reads via unsafe.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Big throughput gains for lifetime/aliasing hazards and portability caveats.
caseStudies.lessons: The win is real but only worth it with rigorous lifetime guarantees and heavy testing.

keyTakeaways: unsafe.Pointer is the legal bridge between pointer types and is GC-tracked; uintptr is a plain integer the GC ignores.
Never store a uintptr address across statements — do pointer arithmetic in a single expression and convert back to unsafe.Pointer immediately.
Struct alignment inserts padding; measure with Sizeof/Alignof/Offsetof and order fields large-to-small to shrink structs.
Zero-copy conversions are powerful but introduce lifetime/aliasing and portability hazards — confine unsafe to tiny, documented, well-tested helpers.
